passage:
Tuesday, late. Salma's diary.

I messed up with Elizabeth today. She sent me a photo of her science project and I typed, "wow nice job genius" meaning it as a joke because we tease each other. No emoji, because my thumb slipped. She didn't answer for an hour. Then she wrote, "ok." That's all. I thought, oh no. Did she read it as sarcasm? I could imagine it two ways: me being nice, or me being mean.

So I called her. It took six rings. "I meant it kindly," I said. She laughed, relieved. "I thought you thought it was bad." I'll add a smiley next time. Or just call. 🙂

qa.q: What did Salma type about Elizabeth's science project?
qa.a: Salma typed, "wow nice job genius".

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth answer only "ok"?
qa.a: She may have read the message as sarcastic and felt hurt or unsure, since there was no smiley and no voice to show the tone. Salma guessed this and called.

qa.q: What could Salma do in future to avoid this?
qa.a: Add a smiley or a clarifying line, or call when the tone might be unclear.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt when only 'ok' came back?
qa.a: Salma felt a jolt of worry, 'oh no', that the joke had read as sarcasm, which is why Salma called instead of texting again.

grounding: A joking message reads as rude because face and voice are missing, and a call clears it up.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi laugh at Yash's first message, and how did Rashmi feel afterwards?

qa.q: What could either of them do next time to avoid the mix-up?

passage:
In the small town of Bhor, the Sunday cricket match ended with Siddharth run out on the last ball. His team lost by one run.
That evening Ojas texted him: "nice job genius"
Siddharth stared at it. He was already feeling terrible. Was Ojas mocking him? He typed, "Thanks for rubbing it in," and threw the phone on the bed.
Ojas saw the reply and frowned. He'd meant it as a joke between them, the way they always teased. But without his grin and his voice, it looked cruel.
He didn't type another message. He called.
"Siddharth, I was joking. Badly. I know you feel bad. That run-out could've happened to anyone. The umpire was blind anyway."
There was a pause, then a small laugh on the line.
"Next time," Siddharth said, "add a laughing face or something."
"Or just call. Calls are better."

qa.q: How many runs did Siddharth's team lose by?
qa.a: His team lost by one run.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he read "nice job genius"?
qa.a: Siddharth felt hurt and humiliated, already upset about the run-out, and read the text as mocking.

qa.q: What did Ojas do that fixed the misunderstanding?
qa.a: Instead of texting again, he called, explained it was a bad joke, and acknowledged Siddharth's feelings.

qa.q: How did Ojas see his own message at first?
qa.a: He meant it as their usual friendly teasing and only realised from the reply that, without his grin and voice, it looked cruel.

grounding: The scene shows a joking message read as rude without face or voice, and a phone call clearing it up.

passage:
It was late in Toronto when Nadia typed to Bilal: "lol I think we're moving to Calgary."
She added the "lol" because she didn't know how else to say it. She'd been crying for an hour.
Bilal replied fast: "haha sure, and I'm moving to the moon 🚀"
Nadia's throat tightened. She put the phone face down and didn't answer.
Bilal waited. Nothing. Usually she'd send a joke back. He scrolled up, read her message again. The "lol" looked strange now. Why would she joke about that?
He typed, "wait. are you serious?" Then deleted it and called.
"Nadia? Sorry. I thought you were joking. Are you actually moving?"
She was quiet, then said, "Yeah. Dad's job. In June."
"That's huge. I'm really sorry I laughed."
They stayed on the phone for an hour.

qa.q: Where was Nadia's family moving?
qa.a: To Calgary.

qa.q: Why did Nadia add "lol" to her message?
qa.a: Nadia felt sad and unsure how to say something so big, so the "lol" softened it, even though she'd been crying.

qa.q: What could Nadia and Bilal try next time a message feels unclear?
qa.a: Add a clarifying line, like "I'm serious," or call, as Bilal did, instead of guessing the tone.

qa.q: How might Bilal have felt when he realised she was serious?
qa.a: He probably felt guilty and embarrassed for laughing, and wanted to make it right, which is why he called.

grounding: The scene shows a serious message read as a joke because of a "lol," and a call clarifying the real feeling.

passage:
Binita had just become secretary of the school's eco club. On Monday she posted in the club group: "Meeting at 5. Be on time. Bring your notebooks."
Within minutes, Himani messaged her privately. "Um, are you angry with everyone?"
Binita was confused. "No? Why?"
"It sounds like a teacher telling us off. Short sentences. Full stops. Some of the juniors think they're in trouble."
Binita read it again. In her head it had sounded efficient. On the screen, with no smile, it looked stern.
She added a second message: "Hi all! Just to be clear, nobody's in trouble 🙂 Excited for our first meeting. See you at 5, and bring notebooks for ideas."
Three juniors sent hearts within a minute.
At the meeting, a Class 8 boy said, "I thought you were going to scold us."
"Me too, apparently," Binita laughed.

qa.q: What time was the eco club meeting?
qa.a: The meeting was at 5.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when Himani asked if she was angry?
qa.a: Binita felt confused and surprised, since in her head the message had sounded efficient, not stern.

qa.q: What did Binita do that worked?
qa.a: She added a friendly clarifying message with a smile emoji, making clear nobody was in trouble.

qa.q: How did the juniors first read Binita's message?
qa.a: They read the short sentences and full stops as a stern telling-off and thought they were in trouble.

grounding: The scene shows a neutral message misread as angry without face or voice, and an emoji and clarifying line fixing it.

passage:
Hi Mehak,
I'm writing this properly because my text last night came out all wrong. When you said you couldn't come to the birthday dinner because of your cousin's engagement, I wrote "wow thanks for nothing". In my head I said it in the voice of our old maths teacher, the dramatic one, and I was grinning. On your screen it was just four cold words. You replied "ok sorry" and then nothing, and I realised you thought I was actually angry. I wasn't. I was disappointed for about five seconds, then happy that you'll be at an engagement with the famous dancing uncle. Next time I'll add a 😜 or just call you when it matters. Can I ring you after school today? I'm saving you a piece of cake either way, the corner one with extra icing.
Uday

qa.q: What did Uday text when Mehak couldn't come?
qa.a: Uday texted "wow thanks for nothing".

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when typing the text?
qa.a: Uday was only briefly disappointed and mostly playful, grinning at the dramatic teacher voice; the letter shows worry afterwards about having hurt Mehak.

qa.q: What could Uday do to avoid this next time?
qa.a: Add an emoji or a clarifying line to show the joke, or call when something matters, since the voice and the grin never reach the screen. 🙂

qa.q: What was 'ok sorry' likely to mean from Mehak's side?
qa.a: Mehak most likely read the four words as real anger and felt hurt or guilty, answering with a short apology and went quiet.

grounding: It shows a joking message reading as rude without face and voice, and a clarifying letter and a call being used to repair it.
